title: Cairo strips 66‑metre Tutankhamun and Nefertiti mural before Xi Jinping visit
content:
A row erupted in Cairo after city authorities removed a 66‑metre‑long mural depicting Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti from view on the eve of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit. The painting, which was part of a set of 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for the visit, was created by the volunteer youth group Rasmet Basma in Tahrir Square.

The mural was removed because it allegedly revived Afrocentric claims about the origins of the pharaohs, a controversy that prompted the authorities to act before the president’s arrival. The removal was carried out to keep the mural out of the esteemed guest’s line of sight.
summary: City authorities removed a 66‑metre mural depicting Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti with dark skin, painted by volunteer youth group Rasmet Basma in Tahrir Square. The mural was one of 40 commissioned to beautify Cairo for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit and was taken down amid allegations it revived Afrocentric claims about the pharaohs’ origins.

content:
Manchester City will launch an appeal as the legal fallout from alleged financial breaches expands.

content:

content: Protesters disrupted a football match between Ireland and Austria, interrupting play with a display that included tennis balls and Palestine flags. title: Shoko Kawata, Japan's first mayor on maternity leave, joins TIME100 Next list
content:
Shoko Kawata, Japan’s first mayor to take maternity leave, has been named to the TIME100 Next list. Her inclusion highlights the historic nature of her decision to step away from municipal duties while expecting a child.

Kawata’s leave sparked mixed reactions across Japan, a nation currently grappling with efforts to raise its birth rate. The public response reflects the broader debate over work‑life balance and family policies in the country.
summary: Shoko Kawata became Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave and was named to the TIME100 Next list. Her leave drew mixed reactions in Japan, a country struggling to lift birth rates.

content:

content: Flydubai pilot Capt Smit Machchhar recounted a cockpit attack by the co‑pilot, saying he intervened to prevent further casualties. The captain told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi that he opened the cockpit door to allow other crew members inside during the incident.

content:

content:

summary: President Trump called Texas Senate GOP candidate Ken Paxton a “pain in the ass” and “a little controversial” during stops in Texas and Oklahoma. He made the remarks weeks before the November elections.

content:
The government is considering a proposal to end charges that require parents to pay extra to sit next to their children on airline flights.  

According to the government, the current policy can cost a parent and child up to £104 for a return journey.
summary: The government is moving to end charges for parents to sit with their children on flights. It says the current cost for a parent and child to sit together can be up to £104 on a return journey.

title: Increased air pollution linked to more night-time coughing, UK‑led study finds
content:
New research led by the University of Cambridge has found that increased air pollution is associated with more frequent night-time coughing, which can disrupt sleep. The study, led by Prof Cecilia Mascolo, highlights that while most air pollution research focuses on severe symptoms requiring medical attention, day-to-day effects are often overlooked.

Prof Mascolo, who hails from a highly polluted area in Italy, noted the significance of these understudied impacts. She stated, “I come from an area in Italy with very high pollution and I am very aware of its not-talked-about effects.” The findings suggest that the link between harmful emissions and sleep disturbance is a critical aspect of air pollution research.
summary: A UK‑led study found that higher air pollution levels are linked to increased night‑time coughing and disrupted sleep. Researchers noted that day‑to‑day symptoms of pollution are often overlooked and the study was led by Prof Cecilia Mascolo of the University of Cambridge.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Japan team transplants human pituitary tissue into primate, boosting cortisol
content:
Researchers in Japan have transplanted pituitary tissue grown from human stem cells into a primate that had its pituitary gland surgically removed, boosting the animal’s cortisol levels. The transplant successfully restored critical hormone signals.

The study was led by researchers from Nagoya University in Japan. In addition to the primate experiment, the team demonstrated that the same method worked in mice over a longer period.
summary: Researchers in Japan transplanted pituitary tissue grown from human stem cells into a primate whose pituitary gland had been surgically removed, restoring critical hormone signals. The team from Nagoya University also demonstrated that the same approach worked in mice over a longer period.

title: First clitoral reconstruction surgery developed for vulvar cancer patients
content:
A new clitoral reconstruction procedure has been developed for women who lose part of their clitoris due to vulvar cancer. This surgical technique marks the first time such a reconstruction has been created, arriving 40 years after the introduction of the first penile reconstruction surgery.

Initial results for the first group of patients treated with this procedure are encouraging.
summary: A clitoral reconstruction procedure has been developed for the first time for women who lose part of their clitoris because of vulvar cancer. Results in the initial group of patients are encouraging, 40 years after the first penile reconstruction surgery.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Metal-organic interactions key to carbon cycling, improving climate change predictions
content:
Metal‑organic interactions have been identified as a key factor in carbon cycling, potentially improving predictions of carbon dynamics under climate change.  

The global annual amount of carbon dioxide (CO₂) released through microbial decomposition of soil organic carbon is estimated to be roughly five times greater than anthropogenic CO₂ emissions.  

This disparity underscores the importance of understanding how climate change influences soil CO₂ release dynamics.
summary: The global annual amount of CO₂ released through microbial decomposition of soil organic carbon is estimated to be about five times greater than anthropogenic CO₂ emissions. This highlights the importance of understanding how climate change affects soil CO₂ release dynamics.
author: Phys.org

title: GRAPES-3 muon telescope finds thunderclouds generate extreme potentials and explains detection bias
content:
A team using the GRAPES‑3 muon telescope, originally designed to study cosmic rays, has discovered that thunderclouds can generate electrical potential differences larger than any direct measurement has recorded. The instrument’s observations revealed a surprising asymmetry: it detected many more thunderstorm events in the eastern portion of its field of view than in the western portion.

The new study, published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics, explains the cause of this imbalance. The research confirms that the GRAPES‑3 telescope is a powerful tool for probing the intense electric fields that develop inside thunderstorms.
summary: An instrument built to study cosmic rays, the GRAPES-3 muon telescope, has shown that thunderclouds can develop electrical potential differences far greater than those ever measured directly. The study also explains why the telescope detected many more thunderstorm events in the eastern part of its field of view than in the western part.
author: Phys.org

title: Underwater Umbrellas Could Shield Coral Reefs from Heat Damage
content: High sea temperatures driven by the climate crisis damage corals, bleaching them ghostly white and killing them. While restoration of dead reefs is possible, it is difficult and expensive, and restored corals remain vulnerable to future heat waves. Finding ways to stop or slow the damage to existing reefs is crucial.
summary: High sea temperatures cause coral bleaching and death. Restoration is expensive and vulnerable to future heat waves, so protecting existing reefs is crucial.
author: Phys.org

title: Medical helicopter crash on Catalina Island kills pilot, nurse; two injured, one missing
content:
A medical helicopter crashed on Catalina Island in California, leaving two people dead, two injured and one still missing. The operator of the aircraft said the fatalities were its own staff members: the pilot and an onboard nurse.

Transport safety officials confirmed that an investigation into the crash is ongoing. The two injured individuals were taken to hospital, while authorities continue to search for the missing person.
summary: A medical helicopter crashed on California's Catalina Island, killing the pilot and an onboard nurse, who were staff members of the operator. Two other people were hospitalized and one remains missing while transport safety officials continue the investigation.

title: Marco Rubio clears $320 million Egypt military aid withheld over human rights concerns
content:
U.S. Senator Marco Rubio approved a waiver that releases $320 million in military aid to Egypt that had been withheld because of human‑rights concerns. The waiver clears the funds for delivery while keeping the issue on the diplomatic agenda.

Rubio said Washington’s concerns about Egypt’s human‑rights record will continue to be addressed in broader bilateral discussions between the two countries.
summary: Top US diplomat Marco Rubio signed a waiver that unblocked $320 million in military aid to Egypt that had been withheld over human rights concerns. He said Washington’s concerns about Egypt’s human‑rights record will continue to be discussed in full bilateral talks.

title: ICE issues guidance tightening vehicle stop rules and banning high‑speed chases
content:
New ICE guidance announced in a memo tightens rules for vehicle stops and bans officers from conducting high‑speed chases.  

The guidance was issued as the Trump administration faces mounting criticism over a series of deadly incidents involving ICE officers.  

ICE officials downplayed the measures, describing them as “mere reminders” and stating that existing protocols will continue.
summary: ICE released new guidance that tightens rules for vehicle stops and bans officers from conducting high‑speed chases. The agency said the measures are merely reminders and that existing protocols will remain in place despite criticism of recent deadly incidents involving ICE officers.

title: G20 trade ministers deadlocked on industrial overcapacity, US trade chief says
content:
G20 trade ministers were unable to reach an agreement on how to address excess industrial capacity and the removal of forced labour from supply chains, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Thursday.

Speaking at the G20 talks in Milwaukee, Greer highlighted the overcapacity issue, a criticism that is often directed at China, which has rejected the claim. He also noted the lack of consensus on eliminating forced labour from global supply chains.

The United States, which holds this year’s rotating G20 presidency, said the deadlock underscores the challenges facing the group.
summary: G20 trade ministers failed to reach agreement on tackling excess industrial capacity and eliminating forced labour from supply chains, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Thursday. Greer made the remarks during talks in Milwaukee, and the United States holds this year's rotating G20 presidency.
author: France 24

title: EU monitor reports record 52% of Europe faced intense heat stress this summer
content:
A record 52% of Europe experienced intense heat stress this summer, the EU’s climate monitor reported on Friday.  

The monitor linked the widespread heatwaves to climate change and noted tens of thousands of excess deaths across the continent. Europe recorded its third‑warmest summer on record, while western Europe saw its hottest conditions, with several nations breaking national temperature records.  

The findings highlight the extent of heat stress that affected more than half of the European region this summer.
summary: A record 52% of Europe faced intense heat stress this summer, according to the EU’s climate monitor on Friday. Europe experienced its third warmest summer overall and its hottest summer in western Europe, with several countries setting national temperature records.
author: France 24

title: Saudi-led coalition says Houthis hit Medina power station serving Prophet's Mosque
content:
The Saudi‑led coalition said on Thursday that Yemen’s Iran‑backed Houthis struck an electricity distribution station that supplies the Prophet’s Mosque in the holy Saudi city of Medina.  

The coalition’s statement said the drone attack drew condemnation across the Muslim world.  

The Houthis denied involvement in the strike, which occurred as fighting intensified between Yemen’s government forces and rebels.
summary: The Saudi-led coalition said Yemen’s Iran‑backed Houthis struck an electricity distribution station that supplies the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina. The Houthis denied involvement in the drone attack as fighting intensified between government forces and rebels in Yemen, prompting condemnation across the Muslim world.

content:

title: EU ministers consider return hubs and stronger Frontex, Greece eyes asylum suspension
content:
EU ministers are discussing new measures aimed at curbing irregular migration, according to recent proposals.  

The plans call for the establishment of “return hubs” outside the European Union and for a strengthening of the EU border agency Frontex. Greece has also suggested that, in emergency situations, asylum applications be temporarily suspended.  

These proposals illustrate the ministers’ focus on tightening migration controls within the bloc.
summary: EU ministers are considering proposals that include setting up return hubs outside the EU and strengthening the border agency Frontex. Greece has proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency situations.
author: DW World

title: Turkey stock scandal affects half a million, prompts arrests and AKP resignation
content:
Turkey’s stock market manipulation scandal has impacted nearly half a million investors, according to recent reports.

Police have carried out several arrests in connection with the scheme, and a female politician from the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) has resigned amid the fallout.

The developments highlight the scale of the alleged fraud and the political repercussions it has triggered.
summary: Nearly half a million investors have been affected by a stock market manipulation scandal in Turkey. Police have made several arrests and a female ruling‑party (AKP) politician has resigned.
author: DW World

title: Ukraine and South Korea dispute over transfer of two North Korean POWs
content:
A diplomatic scandal has erupted after two North Korean prisoners of war were transferred, prompting South Korea to demand an apology from Ukraine.  

South Korea’s demand centers on the handling of the two prisoners, which it says requires an official apology from the Ukrainian government.  

The source does not provide details on how Kyiv has responded to the South Korean demand.

title: Flávio Bolsonaro seeks presidency in Brazil's first-round election as his father remains jailed
content:
Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips reported on Brazil’s historic presidential elections held on Sunday, marking the first round of the nation’s vote. The election features Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, as a candidate with genuine hopes of victory.

Jair Bolsonaro was convicted in September 2025 of attempting a coup and is currently incarcerated. Flávio Bolsonaro is campaigning not only for his own election but also to secure his father’s release.
summary: Brazil’s first round of presidential elections is taking place on Sunday, as reported by Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips. Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro who was convicted in September 2025 of attempting a coup, is campaigning with genuine hopes of victory and to secure his father’s release.
author: Guardian World

title: Brazil's patron saint Our Lady of Aparecida becomes key issue in presidential race
content:
Fears are mounting that Brazil’s patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, could become a decisive factor in the country’s presidential election. Speculation has arisen that candidate Flávio Bolsonaro may attempt to strip the saint of her position, a move some say could influence voter sentiment ahead of the Sunday vote.

The controversy, described as a “row of Biblical proportions,” has turned the saint into an unlikely kingmaker in a race that remains deadlocked. The debate over the saint’s status has drawn significant attention as the election approaches.

Ahead of the Sunday ballot, the two frontrunners – incumbent left‑wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far‑right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro – are level in the polls.
summary: Speculation that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to strip Our Lady of Aparecida of her position has sparked a row in the run‑up to Brazil’s presidential election. The contest pits president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against Flávio Bolsonaro, who are level in the polls ahead of Sunday’s vote.

content:

title: Newly discovered cell type helps shape blood vessel growth in the heart
content:

The discovery was made through experiments conducted with zebrafish. The findings indicate that this newly identified cell type contributes to both the development of the heart and its response to injury.
summary: Researchers have discovered a new cell type that may help regulate blood vessel growth in the heart during development and in response to injury, according to a study from Weill Cornell Medicine. title: Counteranions tune magnetism in copper complexes via molecular packing
content:
Counteranions reshape molecular packing to tune magnetism in copper complexes

The magnetic behavior of copper complexes can be altered by changing the counteranions that surround them, according to new research. The study highlights how the arrangement of molecules in the solid state influences magnetic properties.

Magnetic properties in molecular materials depend not only on the molecular components themselves but also on their solid‑state organization. In charged π‑electronic systems, electrostatic and dispersion forces can organize molecules into distinct ion‑pairing structures, thereby affecting their magnetic characteristics.

These findings underscore the role of counteranions in tuning magnetism in copper complexes.
summary: Magnetic properties in molecular materials depend on both molecular components and solid-state organization. In charged π-electronic systems, electrostatic and dispersion forces organize molecules into distinct ion-pairing structures.

content:

content:
High‑school protests in the northern Paris suburb of Saint‑Denis have escalated, prompting Erin Ogunkeye to welcome a teacher who agreed to speak anonymously. The teacher says the demonstrations are a response to long‑standing problems that have been ignored, and that the students’ demands are not abstract political claims but a call for a learning environment that allows them to succeed.

Police have responded to the protests with teargas and strong‑arm tactics, while students blockaded school entrances in an effort to draw attention to their grievances. The teacher notes that these actions highlight the everyday conditions in which students are expected to learn.

The students’ fundamental demand is for the same opportunities as those in more privileged areas, seeking an environment that supports effective learning.
summary: Protests have intensified at a high school in a northern Paris suburb, with police using tear gas and strong‑arm tactics as students block entrances. Students, speaking through an anonymous high‑school teacher, are demanding an environment that lets them learn effectively and offers the same opportunities as peers in more privileged areas.

title: Fake BBC report falsely implicates Indian passenger and pilot in Flydubai hijacking attempt
content:
A false “BBC” report has circulated online, claiming that an Indian passenger was involved in an attempted hijacking of a Flydubai flight between Dubai and Tel Aviv and that he was linked to the stabbed pilot, Smit Machchhar.

The videos were released after the incident and are AI‑generated deepfakes. The BBC never broadcast the footage, and both the video and audio were doctored. A second clip was also misrepresented; it was filmed in Dubai, not over the location where the incident occurred.

The misinformation was debunked by fact‑checker Vedika Bahl in her “Truth or Fake” segment.
summary: A fake BBC report falsely claims an Indian passenger was behind an attempted hijacking of a Flydubai flight between Dubai and Tel Aviv and links him to the stabbed pilot, Smit Machchhar. The video is an AI-generated deepfake that the BBC never broadcast, and a second clip was misrepresented and filmed in Dubai rather than at the incident location, as fact‑checked by Vedika Bahl in Truth or Fake.

title: Parvati Nair says UK-France migration deal is a diplomatic scheme post-Brexit
content:

Ogunkeye described the deal as a small but revealing element of the broader post‑Brexit relationship, noting that migration questions are intertwined with diplomacy, security, intelligence and surveillance.

She warned that the scheme risks trivialising a complex human plight into deterrence and a numbers game. Ogunkeye argued that humans have always moved and that migration can profoundly enrich societies. The challenge, she said, is to build systems that recognise both national sovereignty and human dignity.
summary: Erin Ogunkeye welcomed Parvati Nair, Professor of Hispanic, Cultural and Migration Studies at Queen Mary University of London, and said the UK‑France migration agreement is a small but revealing element of a wider post‑Brexit relationship. content:
